utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours, and good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Djordjevic. If we --

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The -- who were the persons who were the accused persons in the Bitiqi brother's trial that you testified in? Just the names, please.

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that one of them was Popovic, and I don't know the other's name, but they are two police officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And I think part of the allegations were that the -- the three brothers were removed from custody at a police station or gaol in Prokuplje and taken to Petrovo Selo, a police base at Petrovo Selo. Is that correct, and if so, who arranged for them to be moved?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct that those are the three persons. They had been fined for a misdemeanour, and they were kept in prison. The municipal prison at Prokuplje, they were serving their sentence, and the decision for them to be moved was taken by the minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Who did he -- well, who arranged for them to be transported from Prokuplje to Petrovo Selo?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spoke about that to the investigating magistrate over there, and I answered questions about it. It was my task to call up Goran Radosavljevic and pass on to him the minister's instruction that he should organise their transportation from Prokuplje to the training centre over there. As I couldn't reach him, I passed on that instruction to Popovic, who was one of the officers at the centre at the time who he happened to be there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That's the training centre at Petrovo Selo?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So on your instructions the three boys were handed over to -- to Popovic, Sreten Popovic?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They weren't handed over to Sreten Popovic following my instruction. I informed Sreten Popovic that he should go to Prokuplje and take over those three persons, and others, as was established in the proceedings there, forwarded instructions to the SUP in that territory that the -- those people should be handed over to Popovic and that he should see to it that they be transported.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And this was in July 1999?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And I think you said that was your last involvement in respect to these three persons?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I just gave that instruction to Popovic, and he later went and completed the task, and he took the persons to his training centre where he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That's at Petrovo Selo -- or Selo. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, Petrovo Selo.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And the bodies of these three persons were later found in 2001 in one of the mass graves at Petrovo Selo. Is that what happened later?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I learned as much from the press later.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yesterday -- or not yesterday. I think on Monday you were asked some questions while you were giving evidence in chief, and you gave an answer which indicated that you're aware that the bodies that SUP Chief Keric called and spoke to you about were from Kosovo. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first information from Chief Keric was that there were some bodies, and once he had conducted more detailed checks and established who they were, I, following the information received from him, came to the conclusion that those bodies were from Kosovo based on what he had told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And in discussing this event -- or not this particular event but events of the bodies being concealed at Batajnica, buried at Batajnica, you said that the minister warned you to be careful what you were doing. This was a serious matter. I was wondering what you meant by that. Was the minister threatening you at that stage?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that moment I understood that to be a serious threat.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You mean -- what did you consider he could do to you if you failed to abide by his instructions?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I feared for my own life then, nothing else, and that's how I understood his warning, to keep my mouth shut and not speak about it and that I should do what he was ordering me to.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You thought that the minister was capable of doing you harm to the extent where you could be killed because you might have exposed what was going on?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's how I understood it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did the minister in the past give you any indication or any reason to think that he was so dangerous a person?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If he tells me to be careful what I'm doing and think of myself, he certainly wasn't -- didn't mean that my job was at stake but, rather, something very serious.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, but, you know, there are threats from some people and there are threats from other people. You took this one seriously apparently. Did the minister, by anything he did or say, or anything you knew about the minister, was there anything that caused you to think that the minister was willing and able to carry out the threat?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think at those times of war and even later life in Serbia wasn't very expensive. You could get killed. It was very rough immediately after the war. There were many bodies in both territories, and if you want to achieve something and get a witness out of the way, and at the time there also were political assassinations and attempted murders of political leaders or journalists or some high-profile politicians. I lived in Serbia then, and I was aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: But in 1999, were you then aware of the minister having been involved in that sort of thing?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know that he was involved in anything. I merely received a threat from him which I took very seriously, and it was about my bodily integrity. And bearing in mind all the events of that time, the only possible conclusion for me was to obey and keep silent or I wouldn't fare well in my estimate. And when I say that, I mean I wouldn't fare well physically.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said that he told you -- or if I could start over. After the first two truckloads were -- were buried by -- by the person in charge of the Batajnica base, a few days later he called you again, and that there were two occasions following that first occasion when he called you about other trucks being at the base with bodies to be disposed of. Do you know on those two occasions how many trucks we're talking about?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure which situation you're referring to now. I was called by the minister, and he said to me after the initial burial of the two truckloads from the Danube, he called me and said, "There are trucks over there. Call the officer that we spoke about here and tell him to do the same." So the minister gave me that instruction that the bodies that already had been brought there should be buried.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes. And earlier you said, and this is at 9732 of the transcript, that he called you in respect to more trucks on two occasions after the first occasion. Well, firstly, was it only two occasions after the first occasion, or is it possible that there were more occasions?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whether who called me?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The minister. The minister.

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, then say so. The minister called me twice and told me what I related to you a minute ago, that there were some trucks there already and that I should call that officer and pass on to him that he should proceed as earlier. That's what I received from the minister. And I did call the officer there and passed it on to him, related to him that he should proceed as earlier, and that's what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay. Just to be clear about the sequence, there was the first occasion when he called you at -- in respect to trucks at Batajnica, and then there were two occasions after that. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now I'll repeat for the third time, and you keep asking me the same thing for the third time. Here's what I'm saying. The first time when the bodies were brought where they were brought to Batajnica, the minister called me and said, "Two trucks are at that centre," and they had been brought there earlier from the Danube. "Find the officer and tell him to get the job done." I carried out the order, and after that the minister called me two more times and tells me that there are two or three more trucks. That's what he said to me then. So he called me twice. And I should forward the order that the previous procedure should be repeated, and that's what I did. I called the officer, related that to him, and he did the job.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: On all of these occasions, these three occasions, do you know how many trucks in all were involved?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Caslav Golubovic testified ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. Golubovic testified that he served as your subordinate for years, and I think the word he used was "correct." He always knew you to be correct and professional, and from time to time when he was in Serbia he would -- he would sometime pop by your office. He also testified that he told you that among the bodies found at Bor there were male and female victims. Did he tell you that?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't doubt that he probably told me that too. He spoke to me about those bodies, the way they were dressed, which all points to what I've already said. I suppose that he gave that information to me also. There is no reason why he shouldn't have.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And he also said that he told you that there were one or more children. Did he -- do you recall him telling you that?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose that he told me what he knew at that moment. He spoke about 20 or 30 bodies having been found, but how many children were among them, or women or men, he wasn't able to state in numeric terms. I suppose that there would have been female bodies among them too, but whether there were children and how many, he can't have known at the moment. He may have just given me a general figure, a total figure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I believe that these are very important issues, and it would be good if the exact words that anybody said to Mr. Djordjevic should be quoted literally, because we are dealing with some details. Mr. Djordjevic is being asked whether he remembers or he doesn't remember. So when somebody's words are being related, they should be quoted accurately for him to be able to confirm or deny.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Unfortunately, as you see, the witness commenced his answer by saying, "I suppose that he told me what he knew at the moment." The witness has no accurate recollection of the conversation, as I understand his evidence. Carry on, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And what I put Mr. Golubovic to have said was at 1736 of the transcript. Were you aware of how the arrangements were made to send down the truck from Belgrade to pick up the bodies in Bor?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Before that, I told the minister for the last time that I had been informed that they need one more truck over there because they have no more trucks. Caslav Golubovic's phone -- or phone number is so-and-so, and I no longer want to take part in this, and from that moment on I had nothing to do with any additional transport until the day when the minister called me up and gave me the orders that we have already mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you instruct Mr. Borisav -- well, before we -- you had a chef de cabinet at the time, and if so, was his name?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Slobodan Borisavljevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Was he actually a lawyer as well?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He was a graduate of the military academy.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did -- what did his duties as chef de cabinet entail?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: His duties were to collect all reports from this -- the duty centre, the operations centre, and in the morning he would brief me about the content of those reports. He was also duty-bound to process any documents that were sent from various administrations to be signed, as well as drafting dispatches for me to sign and to send them on to the administrations. That is the entire correspondence, the mail. Daily I would sign mail for two hours in the afternoon. We had a great many employees and much work. So his role was, first and foremost, to handle and process documents, prepare them for me to sign or forward them to the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Was he also responsible to monitor local and international media reports and filter the information that might be important to you?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. His duty was in relation to the documents that he received from the secretariat of the interior to inform me of them and not to go through the foreign press.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, from -- from where would you receive information? Not just the foreign press. I understand that as chief of the public security department you would have a media office. You would have people monitoring the press, wouldn't you? Not just the foreign but local, what is happening in the media. If he's not the person, who was?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I received newspapers daily in the morning. There would be papers waiting for me at my desk, and I would skim through them, and I'm referring to the local newspapers. I'm not sure what you're referring to. In my office I only had the chef de cabinet and the administrative secretary. They were the staff that I had at my disposal. I didn't have anyone else. That was the extent of my office.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The -- did the -- the MUP then, the headquarters of the MUP, including the minister's office, have a section that monitored the media? I ask you because this is, to my understanding, a normal thing for most large police organisations in the world.

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Attached to the minister there was the public relations media office, and I think that they followed and monitored foreign and domestic press and informed the minister thereof. I did not have a service of that sort, and this was not within my competence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you receive any briefings from them?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Their duties were toward the minister, not me. Whatever they prepared for the minister and whatever they had to do based on his request was intended for him. I could not issue any orders or any requests to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes. I was really asking if you received from them press briefings or press clippings.

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I see. Back to Mr. Borisavljevic. How long was he your chef de cabinet?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He had been chef de cabinet of the earlier chief of service and Deputy Minister Stojicic since I was the acting incumbent following his death several months later. He kept his duty as chef de cabinet of the chief of the sector, he had been appointed beforehand and continued in his duty which spanned from 1997, throughout the war, and he stayed with the minister's office even after the war, I believe. I know that definitely he was transferred to the minister's office and that for a while Zoran Alimpic was chef de cabinet, my chef de cabinet.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you find him to be trustworthy and reliable?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I trusted people as a rule, so I placed my trust in him as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You entrusted him with the task of doing the paperwork to cover the operational expenses for the workers who had retrieved the bodies in Bor, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you tell him what it was about?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that he knew what this was about even earlier on. The paper that the chief of the SUP had sent to the administration of the crime police, and they in turn sent a request to my office because they were in need of these special operative resources. So that paper was written by him. He dispensed the necessary money to the crime police administration, and this money was subsequently used as remuneration for the workers at Bor. I'm not sure which of the papers he handled. I know that he dealt with the operative procedure for expenses, but I can't tell you which documents he specifically produced and what they were about.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can we look at 05227. That's a 65 ter number. And it's P391.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: This is a request for your approval of the payment of 10.000 dinars for the operational expenses incurred, dated the 22 of April 1999. Before we look at this document, it was Mr. Golubovic, according to his testimony, who told you that they needed $10.000 to pay these workers. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And the name of the operation was Dubina II. You are -- or who was it who dubbed the operation Dubina II?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't dub it. And as for the action itself, well, I'm really not familiar with the name at all, Dubina II. As the letter before us states -- it's not clear to me. I don't know who initiated the action, who named it. I am really in the dark on that. I suppose that at the time I was signing this I didn't pay much attention to it. I knew what the money was intended for, and the name of the action obviously did not interest me at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. How did Major General Ilic, who signed the request, become involved in this activity?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He only had to do with the paperwork level of it. Caslav called me and told me that money had to be obtained. Since it was not possible to use the resources of the secretariat, I told him that he should send a request to the crime police administration since that was the only way in which monies could be transferred as operational expenses. That was the only way to do it in keeping with the law, to go through the crime police administration. So the request was sent to the administration chief and through the office they received the amount of 10.000. Caslav subsequently made sure the workers received the money. The role of the crime police was to credit the money in such a way as to abide by the law.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay. So if we look at P392. This is a payment order on the 22nd of April.

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And if you look at the bottom of it you will see that somebody signed for receipt of the money. Who signed for receipt of the money?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recognise the signature at this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Does it look like --

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot decipher it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Does it look like Mr. Ilic's signature?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly. It could be Ilic's signature. It's possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: At the top it says, To pay to Major General Ilic the sum of 10.000 dinars. Very well. And --

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And if we move to 393, P393. It's a payment of operational expenses for Dubina II document, dated 22nd of April 1999. And if you look at the second page in English and B/C/S, we see where the workers, including -- well, five workers signed for having received the money on the 27th of April. That's the normal documentation for this procedure, is it?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think it's out of the ordinary. The worker who paid out the money had to have the signature of the persons receiving it in order for him to have receipt that they had indeed received money. It could have been done perhaps differently with a special format of receipt.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay. Who -- who is it that signed as having confirmed payment was made on the 27th?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is confirmed by the chief of the OKP, meaning the crime police department of the Bor SUP, presumably. Therefore, the chief of the crime police department from Bor.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay. Do you know who from the ministry carried the money down to Bor?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. Dragan Ilic took over the money, and I can't remember who he handed it over to in order for the money to be paid out in the field. I don't recall who he assigned for that specific task.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Caslav Golubovic said that it was a policeman by the name of Aleksic who was working at the criminal police administration under General Ilic's command. Does that jog your memory, that he ...

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. If that's what Caslav said, then it is likely that Caslav did hand him over the money. There's no reason for me to doubt that the person Aleksic from the crime police administration gave the money to Golubovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you remember Aleksic's first name?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not at this time. I know of an individual, Aleksic, having been there. If you told me, I might recognise the name, but I can't recall it at this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. Now, didn't the minister, either yourself or the minister, task Mr. Ilic and Mr. Aleksic to go down to Kosovo and engage themselves in operations that were referred to as clearing the battle-field or "asanacija"?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a completely different topic now.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, but I'm asking nonetheless. Do you recall that they were sent down to Kosovo? Well, let's break down the question. Do you recall that they were sent down to Kosovo to work down there during the war, both Ilic and Aleksic?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that Dragan Ilic was down there, and I believe that Aleksic was as well, but I know for a fact that Dragan Ilic was there, and I believe he went there twice. The travel order and the task that he was to go about down there was given by the minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you know what the task was?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had a better recollection of the second time when Dragan Ilic came to Belgrade on the 2nd June when I was signing the travel order and his bills. He told me that he had had the task to help and instruct the chiefs of crime police departments to properly conduct crime scene investigations, which ranged from deaths to sites of bombardment. That was the extent of his tasks as he explained them to me. He got in touch with the chief of the staff, the chiefs of crime police departments, and his tasks had, as he put it, mostly to do with upgrading the expertise of the crime police in crime scene investigations, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honours, I wonder if we could go into private session just for a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: K93 was tasked by Assistant Minister Zekovic on quite a few occasions to go and collect corpses [Realtime transcript read in error "corporations"] from various places [Realtime transcript read in error "polices"]. Firstly, did you know K93, and for how long if so?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew him. I don't know for how long. He worked in the service employing drivers, but I knew him, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Were you on speaking terms with him?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was on speaking terms with everyone. Some ten years previously, he would be my driver on some of the business trips I did, but that was the extent of our communication. We would greet each other as work associates, and that was in fact the extent of my communication with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Who was your driver in 1999?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bogdan Lipovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you know who was Mr. Zekovic's driver in 1999?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that Basanovic was his driver for a period of time. He was able to use other drivers too. I don't think he always used that one driver. It depended on the availability of drivers. Basanovic was the driver present in the particular service, and whenever he was available he would drive whoever needed a driver.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness's microphone please be removed a little bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: From his shoulder. I think it rubs on his sleeve.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: While that is happening, on page 16, line 10, the word "corporations" should be "corpses," and the word "polices" should be "places."

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours. That has to be -- to be expunged. I'm so sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you know whether or not K93 was also the driver for Sreten Lukic at some point in time?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. It is possible that he, just as I did, would call upon the service to provide him with a driver, and whoever was available was provided him. I don't think he was specifically assigned to be his driver. It is possible that he was his driver for some of the business trips. I can't be more precise than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: K93 and another witness, K88, testified that Bogdan Lipovac and Basanovic, Dragan Basanovic, were two of the persons who drove some of the trucks with the corpses to Batajnica. Do you know of that?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In May 19 -- I'm sorry, 2001, can you recall participating in a discussion with Mr. Lukic and K93 in Mr. Lukic's office?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After retiring on the 4th until I left on the 12th of May, I came to the office there daily, and I was also at Lukic's office, and it's possible that he also arrived on an occasion when I was there. I cannot rule that out.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: He said that he was involved in an argument with Lukic about his transfer, and you came and joined the argument or the discussion. Do you recall participating in the discussion with Mr. Lukic and K93 regarding his transfer? And when I say "transfer," I mean for him to go to work somewhere outside of Belgrade, in Bujanovac.

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, I was a pensioner, and I had serious problems of my own. So the problems of other people, including Sreten Lukic or the other person, I may have entered when they were having an argument, but I cannot remember what they were spoke -- talking about. I think I saw something like that, but what they talked about -- I came there as a pensioner to take care of some of my own business.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: How long had you known Djordje Keric up to April 1999? That's the SUP chief for Uzice.

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe for a -- for 15 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: He -- well, how long did the operation to retrieve the bodies from Lake Perucac and bury them on the bank of the river, how long did that operation last? Do you recall?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember precisely, but my last contact was when he informed me that apart from the bodies what could be sitting over there were also parts of some sort of a crate, and maybe a day or two later I -- we had a phone conversation when he informed me what had been done with the bodies found. So the procedure there, that is the exhumation of the bodies and their burial close to the dam, took a short period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, he said two days thereabouts. Would that be consistent with your memory?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's possible that it took two days.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: He also said that he was duty-bound to keep you abreast of the developments and that he was in telephone contact with you several times over those two days. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He contacted me twice only, as far as I remember, or three times at the most. So once when he told me that, and after that one more time or two more times. Our last communication was when he informed me about what they had done.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: He said that -- well, do you know the SUP crime chief, what his name was at the time? If I could recall, Zoran Mitricevic or Mitricivic.

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The name of the chief was Zoran Mitricevic, if I'm not mistaken. He was the chief of the criminal police service. I knew his name, although I had no personal contact with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, did you -- at the time when you got the first call from Keric reporting that this truck with the bodies was seen in the lake, did you instruct Keric to send the crime chief, whether by name or just by position, the crime chief for the SUP down there to find out what the situation was?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the chief of the SUP informed me of what he had learned from the people in the field, I just gave orders to conduct additional checks and see what that was all about. That's all I asked of him, to have complete information and be able to inform the minister. I didn't tell him either to send the chief of the criminal police or Zoran Mitricevic or anybody else by name. That was for him to decide. He could have entrusted the department of the interior with that. So I just required him to conduct a detailed check of the situation and how -- but how, that was for him to decide.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. Keric testified that when he received information that the bodies in the box in the -- in the river -- in the lake were increasing, he called you and informed you of that, and you told him that the orders of the minister was that the bodies should be removed from the lake and buried in a grave named Lake Perucac dam. In other words, he said, You convey the minister's orders to bury the bodies in the dam. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't convey to him anything regarding the burial of the bodies. He informed me, and once he had informed me that next to the bodies there was also that box, I passed the information on to the minister, but I received no feedback from the minister, nor did I require Keric to do anything. That being the case, Keric called me, and he informed me what he had done and how. I passed the information on to the minister, and that was all my involvement with Perucac and the bodies that were found there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did Mr. Keric tell you that an attempt had been made to sink the truck, the box, in the dam and that had failed? Not in the dam, in the lake.

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He didn't relate any such detail to me, nor did I elicit such information from him. He informed me of what he had done, and I passed on that information and that was all my involvement.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did he -- I'm sorry. Did you not instruct him that he should not inform the investigating judge and that entire event should be kept as a secret, as secret as possible? Because that's his testimony. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't give him any orders to the effect that he should refrain from informing the Prosecutor or judicial organs. At that moment, I was -- well, in a sort of argument with the minister, and I wanted to be -- to keep out of some things. We have seen that this was one more case which pointed to what had happened on the Danube. I didn't relate to him any details because I wanted to keep out of the entire story, and I have said so already.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you know, since you were at that time in argument with the minister, whether the minister spoke to Keric and told him, gave him the instructions to bury the bodies at the bank of the lake and not to inform the judge or the prosecuting authorities?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether the minister gave orders to anybody with regard to that, nor did Keric say to me when he definitely informed me of what had been done, whether he had received orders to that effect from the minister or anybody else. I didn't know about that at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'd like us to look at a document and -- and see if that jogs your memory. This is 65 ter 06003. And it's a record of the testimony of Zoran Mitricevic before the investigating judge, having been cautioned to speak the truth and warned of the consequence of giving false testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If we could go quickly to page 6 of this record in the English, which is page 5 in the B/C/S. We want to look at the bottom half of page 5 in the B/C/S and the top half of page 6 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Have a read of that, Mr. Djordjevic, from where he refers to Slavko Petrovic and Djordjevic. Not you, but another policeman of the same name who was at Uzice at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we scroll to the top in English, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: He said he went up to the lake with Slavko Petrovic and Djordjevic. There were two -- there was also an inspector, Milutinovic. They could see the refrigerating box that had surfaced on the lake, a freight box which resembled the refrigeration box of a lorry. That there are many bodies inside, that the bodies are dropping out of it, that it had fallen apart in the water and that they were floating on the water. "I immediately informed Chief Keric by phone about this, and he said, Wait until I get instructions from the ministry. And before that when he set off, I said, 'What are we going to do. Yes, Djoko said immediately. I hadn't even informed him.' He said no taking of photos, no record-taking, no informing the judge, prosecutor, nobody whatever. That is the order from above. That is what the chief of department ordered and that is how it has to be done. I informed him that there was no chance of sinking it, nor could it be sunk. So what were we to do next? Then after a few of those calls and discussions he said we should try to pull this out and that this be buried some place, that these were the instructions he got from the MUP." Does this refresh your memory as to the instructions that you gave Mr. Keric?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Should I answer? This doesn't refresh my memory in any way. I never gave any such orders to Keric. I merely said to him that he should check what that was about and inform me so that I could inform the minister. After that, he sent a team that went to the place and they saw what they saw, this box, and after that Keric called and said there were not only bodies on the water but that there was also this box. I received that information from him with the intention of passing it on to the minister, which I did. I didn't give any instructions to Keric, neither to sink the refrigeration box nor to take the bodies out of the water or bury them where they were buried. That's what Keric did after he had informed me but before he had reported to me about what had been done, namely that the bodies had been recovered and buried near the dam. That was the entire communication between Keric and me. Any communication between Keric and Mitricevic is not known to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, now we are treading on ground that is similar to interviews. Statements made by persons who haven't testified here are being used now, and their statements, it wasn't possible to verify them. Still, the Prosecutor is using these statements. We are now tackling the issue of how statements should be dealt with, and there is a pertinent decision made by this Bench, and I'll -- I can say what was decided on the 24th of June this year when I cross-examined, when Ms. Kravetz intervened with regard to Clark's statement. So I believe that only the circumstances can be dealt with and not what Mr. Stamp is doing, namely, quoting. So in accordance with your decision, that's the way how the accused can be questioned. So on the 24th of June, 1999, you made a pertinent decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honours, I could check that, but I was following carefully, and I do not recall any decision to the effect that you could not ask a witness whether or not he could comment on what somebody else has said. That is the question. I'm not trying to tender the statement. I'm not using it as evidence. I just merely say to the witness, "These are what your subordinates have said. What are your comments? Do you now recall having heard that they said this?"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: At the moment, Mr. Stamp, I would not interfere with what you are doing, and it may be possible during the coming break to check exactly the decision referred to by Mr. Djurdjic to see that my memory of it is accurate. Carry on, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you know of any reason that Mr. Keric or Mr. Mitricevic would have to lie about this aspect, that you gave an instructions based on directions you got from the minister to bury the bodies?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That's going too far, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. Could we with your leave, Your Honours, jut go into private session briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic, I'm going to ask you some questions --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Sorry. I'm so sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will adjourn now and resume at five minutes to 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: My apologies that we were delayed coming in. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic, K87 testified or -- testified and gave a statement much consistent to what you have said. He also told us that -- that you instructed him to use -- or to make use of an excavator to dig the hole, and that excavator was obtained with a permit that you provided. Do you recall making those arrangements?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't tell by the number whether it was the officer present there or someone else.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, I think K87 said that someone else, another witness, K88. He went to your office to collect the permit for the excavator, to obtain an excavator from a construction company in Batajnica.

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In other words, I don't know who 87 or 88 are. At any rate, nobody came to see me to obtain a permit for an excavator. At the point in time when I was conveying the order in my office to the person in charge of that facility, the question was raised as to how the matter would be brought to a close. There ensued a discussion concerning the use of an excavator for those purposes. He told me that there was an excavator to be found near the feature, near that facility, and I instructed him that he should go and obtain the excavator in order to do the job. Nobody came to see me later on for any sort of permit or my consent for the use of an excavator because I can't give one to begin with. That's all I remember concerning the use of an excavator.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, first it was cited that one K person said so-and-so, and then the other K person said so-and-so. Can we please quote the statements of these witnesses. And I'm sure that one of the two witnesses, K88, definitely did not say what Mr. Stamp has just cited. It was, rather, the other K who was involved in this discussion. I don't want to influence witness's answer in any way. My remarks have to do with the procedural matter, my objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think from what you have said that you have misunderstood what was said at page 26, line 19. What was said, that K87 said that another person, K88, went to your office. It's not the both of them gave evidence of the same thing, but one of them only said that the other one had gone to the office. Thank you, Mr. Djurdjic. Again, though, Mr. Stamp, we're being reminded that sometimes you are putting matters very loosely. The Defence are concerned of material matters. So as with yesterday, if you would take the time to be more precise. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. And I was reference to P1414, paragraph 13 and paragraph 18. That's what I was citing.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic, K -- did K87 eventually contact you and requested that you stop sending bodies to the SAJ centre?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that at one point in time after the second call he expressed his dissatisfaction with the situation. But it wasn't me who was sending bodies to him. The bodies arrived, and I only conveyed orders. I wasn't pleased with my participation in these events, just as he was not, but that's what the situation was like.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And if we could move on to Mr. Trajkovic. You had worked closely with Mr. Trajkovic for many years going up from 1999, had you not?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Approximately how many years going up to that, 1999?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're probably referring to 1999. It was interpreted back to me as 1990. Up until the time he joined the special unit through to the end of his term there in 2000, I worked closely with him if I could -- I can put it that way. But we were not on unfriendly or hostile terms.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter is not sure. Perhaps the within said "We were not as friends."

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: He said that when K87 told him about the burial, he spoke to you on a couple of occasions about it, and your response was, "What can I tell you? All my brave generals buried their heads into the sand, and they left it to me to finish this part of the work."

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my discussions with he -- him and with Caslav Golubovic and Keric, I clearly expressed my dissatisfaction with the way things were being dealt with. I think that I spoke to him once, not several times after the war, and that time I also expressed my dissatisfaction at having been drawn into it. I didn't say anything of the sort. Perhaps it was his liberal interpretation of the matter. I said that I had been drawn in to doing things contrary to my will and wishes. That was the way I explained my attitude toward it. I didn't have any benefit from it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you also tell him that the decision to -- to bury the bodies there had been made from a very high level?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't use those words. I said that there was someone above me who decided about it, and I did what I did and that's why I'm here.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. Golubovic said that it was not lawful for the police to remove the bodies without an order from the investigating judge. Would you agree with me that the removal of the bodies from Bor was unlawful at the time?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that it was in keeping with the decree which was amended for the times of war in relation to the criminal investigation and examinations done by the police. I think that under that decree certain actions could be taken and subsequently the bodies of the judiciary could be reported to. I can't make an assessment now whether it was in accordance with or contrary to the law.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The burial of the bodies, though, in mass graves in -- let's start with Batajnica. That was unlawful.

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was not in keeping with the regulations.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And also at Lake Perucac, on the banks of the lake. That wasn't in keeping with the regulations either.

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. It was not in keeping with the regulations.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said the minister also -- or that you conveyed an order to Mr. Golubovic to destroy the truck. That was also unlawful.

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, definitely. This order of his whereby he said that when the bodies are transported the refrigerator truck ought to be destroyed, this was a signal to me that I definitely had to take myself out of the entire situation. I could see the turn of the events, that they -- they weren't taking a good turn, and unfortunately it all took a different course afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said that you told the minister on more than one occasion that you wanted to set up a group or a commission to investigate these corpses. Now, did you then realise that that was your duty under the law, to have these corpses that had emerged properly investigated?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. After the first conversation and the order I conveyed to Caslav, on my return to the minister's office I proposed that the case be settled in such a way as to send a team that would inquire into what this was about and where the bodies came from in order to clear up the whole process, to put it that way. He remained silent. He disagreed with my proposal, and it all pointed to the fact that something went wrong. He did not agree with me that a team should be put together in order to elucidate the details and facts surrounding the emergence of these bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: But you realised at that time that that was the proper and lawful thing to do.

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. I knew that the matter had to be approached this way. I proceeded first and foremost from myself. I didn't know what had happened. I didn't know where the bodies had come from. I didn't see what sort of role I was to play in this. That's why I tried to clear the matter up, but things were not done that way. They were done differently.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said that when you had tried to obtain information from the minister he said that certain incidents, certain isolated incidents that happened down there, and something should be done to prevent the revelation or the finding of these bodies which resulted from these incidents. The question is: Did that cause you to become aware that these bodies were the bodies of persons who were the victims of murder or unlawful killing?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to his words, and he told me at the time that these were isolated cases involving deaths, as well as consequences of NATO bombing. That was his response to my insistence that the matter be cleared up, that the matter be elucidated. He said that these were the consequences of bombing, as well as casualties following the fighting with terrorists, as well as isolated cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Isolated cases of what?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of incidents causing deaths of the persons who were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Of murder. Weren't you aware that the reason why the minister wanted these bodies concealed, to use -- to quote you, the minister said that something should be done to prevent the revelation of the finding of these bodies was because these were the bodies of people, at least some of them, who were the victims of murder?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He used the word "incidents." Whether they were murders, my understanding was based on what he said at the time, and he said that there had been isolated cases and that there were other cases that came as a result of NATO bombing. I was not aware of any murders having taken place down there involving the deaths of civilians in greater or smaller numbers. I wasn't aware of any such events.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay. But I was asking you to be reasonable. What conceivable reason could the minister have to be burying the bodies and concealing for years the bodies of persons who were the victims of NATO bombing?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am testifying about what he told me at the time. Now, what his motives and reasons for it were, well, he told me that the main motivation behind this course of action was that it should not become known, NATO… I don’t know, that bodies should not be uncovered, that NATO might use this to justify their bombings and so on. That's how he put it to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No. I just want to make this clear to you what I'm asking. What you, in the position you're at --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think that the last statement was not entered correctly into the transcript. Perhaps Mr. Popovic could draw your attention to what this is about. The matter is English and I'm not in command of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if you'll allow me to state that what I have to do is with line 20. It is said that NATO might be using them as a -- the results of NATO bombings were not mentioned in his answer at all, that they might be using -- NATO might be using it as justification for the results of NATO bombings. But he didn't put it that way. You will see if you listen to the tape that what was said in Serbian was quite different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Popovic. We will have that part of the transcript verified in due course. Thank you. Carry on, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay. I just want to make this clear. We have heard your evidence as to what the minister said and what he told you and also what he did not tell you. What I'm asking you is about what conclusions you drew at the time. What was your state of mind, because that is very important. When -- what -- what reason could the minister have, in your view, to be concealing the bodies of the victims of NATO bombing?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what he told me, but what reason he may have had, I really -- I know that later, sometime during the NATO bombing, he gave orders to file criminal complaints against NATO countries and NATO leaders, and most of them were sentenced to 20 years of prison. That was his struggle. That was his attitude. I couldn't read his mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Based on the position you were in at the time, why or what reason would the minister have, in your view, to be concealing for years the bodies of persons who were killed in alleged anti-terrorist operations?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what conclusion to draw. Acting upon his orders, at one moment I did something of which I didn't approve then, and I don't approve of it now, and it has burdened me for years, but at that moment while the country was being devastated and while people were getting killed in Serbia and everything else we spoke about, I acted the way I did at the moment, and I accepted his orders without opposing them. I'm aware that this was a big mistake I made, but what happened cannot be made undone. I am ashamed of my deeds, and I believe that the Court's decision will be adequate, and I will be held responsible for what I did. I know that I'm not responsible for the death of anybody in Serbia or Kosovo, but that -- the situation was like that. Things happened and I'm here now.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm referring back to what you said, and having regard to your testimony about Mr. Stojiljkovic decision and orders to conceal these truckloads of bodies, weren't you aware that these bodies must have been the victims or these were the corpses of the victims of crimes committed by the police, and that why Mr. Stojiljkovic wanted to conceal them?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, those weren't persons who had lost their lives under normal circumstances but certainly as a consequence of the overall events down there in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay. I'm not saying now that you knew anything about what was going on in Kosovo, so bear with me. Let us, for the -- for now, for the purpose of this question, accept that you don't -- or did not know what was going on in Kosovo. What I want you to do is put yourself back to what was going on in your mind at that period in 1999 when Minister Stojiljkovic said that these bodies were to be concealed. Did you not draw the conclusion, or at least suspect that these were the victims of unlawful conduct by the police in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After some of his orders, I realised that this wasn't due process. This wasn't the normal regular procedure, that there had been victims in Serbia. So the entire procedure was not in line, not in keeping with the laws and regulations, and all that indicated that things were being done that were not regular. And the purpose of those irregular activities, the only conclusion that can be drawn about that is that those -- the intention was for those bodies to be concealed in an irregular manner. That's what I can make of it now. I hope you're satisfied with this answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Partially, but, you know, it requires a little bit more first, before I understand that. Firstly, Mr. Stojiljkovic -- or did you draw the conclusion that Mr. Stojiljkovic would have wanted these bodies concealed because they resulted from crimes or irregular activities of persons that he was responsible for, that is, the police in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't draw any conclusions because there were no elements available to me to do that. I supposed that the cause of death of those persons was what he said to me and possibly something else in addition. So I really had no concrete knowledge about the circumstances in which those people were killed. My assumptions at the moment could have been all sorts of things, but I was certainly aware of the procedure being irregular at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Of course, but just coming back to the question. Didn't you at least suspect that Mr. Stojiljkovic wanted these bodies concealed because they resulted from irregular activities of persons that he was responsible for, that is the police?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, of course I had -- I suspected that the people came to harm in the activities at Kosovo, but I couldn't know how that happened, whether we're speak -- talking about crimes or bombing or something else, but everything indicates what you're assuming, but those were my assumptions, too, that those were bodies of persons who had lost their lives under circumstances I was unfamiliar with then, and I could suppose that they had been killed in one or more of many ways.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, but Stojiljkovic, the minister for the MUP -- and I keep getting back to this. I'd like just to get your answer so we can move on. He's a minister for the police. Didn't you conclude or at least suspect that he wanted these bodies concealed because the killings resulted from police action in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're now making me assume things. I am testifying to what I know and what he told me. These people could have lost their lives in several ways down there. My assumption in this case is that those persons who came to harm were not treated fairly, but how they got killed is not for me to speculate about. I could have suspected this or that, but I really had no information about how they were killed. But certainly the minister's decision to handle the bodies of the people killed down there the way they were handled certainly isn't all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Was there in place -- well, could I ask the question this way: If you had information indicating that the minister, Stojiljkovic, was involved in criminal conduct, were there procedures in place for you as the chief of the police to take action?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I proposed some procedural steps at the beginning, but when I became aware that these were his exclusive prerogatives, after he failed to take relevant decisions I couldn't do anything. I as an individual couldn't elucidate the situation or find out what had happened. When I made those proposals, he didn't accept them, and he made it clear -- or clearly pointed out the limits of my activities and my interest. And my legal -- the legal possibilities and the factual possibilities for me were -- I didn't have any legal or factual possibility to do anything and without his decision and the organs at his disposal.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: But surely, Mr. Djordjevic, if you as police chief, or any policeman in Serbia at the time, had information that a minister might have been committing crimes, reasonable -- or information that would lead you to reasonably believe that the minister might have committed crimes, there must be a procedure that you could follow.

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know which procedure that may have been. If he issues an order to do something and threatens me to mind my own business and that he is responsible for that, at that time when people were getting killed in Serbia I didn't take any other measures. I knew then, as I know now, that it wasn't right, and I'm willing to -- to assume responsibility for a rash action.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, but I'm asking you a more hypothetical question. Just speaking hypothetically, and separate yourself from the -- that particular incident, what procedures would a policeman in Serbia at the time adopt or follow when that policeman had information or allegations that led him reasonably to believe that a person in high office, like a minister of the government, was committing crimes?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All persons are equally responsible for crimes, so whoever commits a crime or any other criminal offence should be treated like anybody else. That's not a contentious issue. So if I knew or if somebody knew of somebody else having committed a crime, that criminal responsibility has to be established and subsequently processed by pressing criminal charges and the rest. That's the regular procedure that follows any -- the reception of any information about criminal offences irrespective of who committed them. I should have acted accordingly, and I would probably have gotten killed and everything would have been all right now and there would be no problems. I didn't act that way, although I assumed that there may have been a crime involved and that the procedure wasn't regular and fair, but I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yeah, precisely. That's reasonable to assume or conclude that a crime was committed. But the fact that it was minister for the MUP, Stojiljkovic, who was concealing the body, must have indicated to you, sir, that possibly it was the police who were committing the crime. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's a mere assumption, whether it was the police or anybody else. I can't know who committed those crimes. Possibly the police. Possibly the citizens killed each other. It may have been due to the bombing. Everything is possible. I had no information about the circumstances in which those people were killed. We saw here in the proceedings that there were really some gruesome situations. Who had committed those misdeeds and crimes. In some instances the perpetrators were police officers. In others they were citizens dressed up in some type of uniform. In other instances again, the military was involved. My conclusions to that effect would be completely arbitrary. I have no information based on which I could infer how those people came to harm from these or -- or other structures.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In your subsequent -- subsequent meetings with the president of Serbia, Mr. Milutinovic, did you mention to him what you told us Mr. Stojiljkovic was doing?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never had a meeting with Milutinovic in four eyes. I only met Mr. Milutinovic when the MUP delegation was led by Minister Stojiljkovic or upon Milutinovic's order when we went to see the president of the SRJ, when he had a meeting with the leaders of the police and the military and some politicians. So I never had a private meeting with Milutinovic, just him and me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you take any steps to inform the president, Milutinovic?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you why I didn't take any steps. That was a time of random destruction, and I was threatened to mind my own life and for all those reasons I opted to keep silent, and I never said anything to anybody until my conversation with Trajkovic, and only after he had said that one of his subordinates had informed him about that.

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I can't tell by the number now, but I suppose that it was the leader of that group that was established to -- to establish the facts about the bodies found. If that's the man, he was mentioning a certain note, then that's a different topic for discussion.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: One moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we go into private session briefly, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, and we'll redact your previous question, Mr. Stamp. That testimony was in closed session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And you were there again on the 17th of February in Pristina for the MUP meeting where Mr. Stojiljkovic and Mr. Lukic, in particular, made presentations on the future plans?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 17th of February, 1999?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was present at the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And you were also there on the 8th of March, 1999, according to Mr. Cvetic.

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't remember being there on the 8th of March.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And you were there at a MUP staff meeting on the 16th of April, 1999.

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And you met, according to Mr. Djakovic, with Mr. Lazarevic on the 18th of April.

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's a different matter altogether.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Sorry. I withdraw that last question. Were you also there on the 18th of April, in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Were you there from the 16th to the 18th or after the 18th?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the morning of the 16th, I set out for the staff meeting with the minister. We got there, had the meeting. The minister held a conference, and we returned to Belgrade thereafter. Already on the 16th in the evening hours, we were in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: When did you return to Kosovo after that?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two days later. Since decisions were handed out on the appointment of certain chiefs of SUP structures and hand-over of duties at the 16th of -- of April meeting, I was given the instruction by the minister to go there and see what was going on. So I left Belgrade on the morning of the 18th, got to Pristina, toured the Pristina SUP and saw the chief who was supposed to be replaced. I finished my meeting with him. I also visited the staff prior to the meeting with him. I also went to Urosevac where I was present during the hand-over of duty between the former and incumbent chief of the SUP. I stayed to talk to them and went back to Pristina. Subsequently, I also met with Generals Pavkovic, Lazarevic, and Djakovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And on these occasions, the 16th and the 19th of April, the 19th in particular because you travelled to -- to Urosevac as well, did you not observe that in many places the villages where the ethnic Albanian population -- population inhabited were in ruins, were burnt?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first of all, I wasn't there on the 19th. I left Belgrade on the morning of the 18th. And it was in the early evening hours that -- on that same day that I went to Belgrade. What I was able to see from the main road and the damage I saw was extensively also in Pristina due to bombing. Pristina was all potholed from bombing. There had been bombing of that area on several occasions. It was not down to me to inquire into the damage and how it was inflicted, the damage on the buildings that I saw. I didn't have occasion to go and tour villages in order to find out the extent of damage and who it was inflicted by. I really wasn't able to deal with that. There was a war on. There was general fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you know that even while you were there on the 18th of April people, that is Kosovo Albanians, were being expelled from -- from Pristina area, from the area around -- from the area in Pristina municipality?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the discussions I had in Urosevac, I asked the chief about the situation and the developments. He told me that movement was noted of civilians, primarily by train to Macedonia, because the railway line goes through Urosevac. And this was something I was able to hear from the reports from Belgrade as well. So I got the following information from the incumbent chief and the former chief of Urosevac. People were on the move because they feared bombing and fighting with terrorists. They feared for their safety, and that's why they decided to leave the territory. I also knew from before, from 1998, that civilians had been on the move depending on where various operations took place. Nobody told me on that occasion that civilians were being driven out or forced out of their flats. What the chief informed me about was in a way confirmation of what I had already known, that citizens were leaving because they feared for their safety on account of bombing. There was no question of these civilians having been driven out by whatever authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: While you were there on any -- well, before we -- I move to that -- you were also there on the 10th of July, 1999, or thereabouts?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was there on the 10th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In July 1999, how many times were you there?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In Kosovo, yes.

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the 10th of June -- or, rather, as of the 10th of June the police forces had been withdrawn and nobody was able to go to Kosovo any longer. But I -- I apologise. I was at the negotiations as a member of the co-ordinating body with the KFOR or NATO forces at the border crossing of Medere. It was a facility belonging to the international forces, and we were discussing the security zone. It may have been in 2001. That was the only time I got into the territory, some 100 metres into the territory, but after that presence of mine in Kosovo earlier on I never went there again.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm just focusing on June and July 1999. How many times did you go to Kosovo in those two months?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In July and June -- well, I was -- the only time I was there was the 10th of June when we had a meeting about the implementation of the agreement with NATO concerning the withdrawal of our forces. So that was my only visit there for the months of June, July, and the subsequent months.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay. Right. And it's the 10th of July, actually, you mean. The transcript says 10th of June.

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. June. It was the month of June, not the month of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I see. Thank you. When you went there in April 1999, did you meet with Obrad Stevanovic?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both times. On the 16th when I was there with the minister, and on the 18th when I got there I met with Obrad Stevanovic. And I also saw him on the 10th of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you ask him or ask Mr. Lukic or any member of the staff if they knew anything about the bodies that the minister directed to be buried in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't discuss any of these matters with them, because under the order or under the request from the minister I was forbidden from discussing the topic with anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Even while you were in Belgrade during this period, March, April, May 1999, you were in contact with them. You could contact them from where you were in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could be in contact with them when the telephone lines were up and running, and I certainly was in contact with them at the time, especially when some of our personnel were killed. I would be in touch with them on that score. Other than that, I didn't have any regular contacts with them. The end -- based on the task I received from the minister, I have not able to give them any orders or tasks. These were primarily brief private conversations, not -- nothing official.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What sort of working relationship did you have with Mr. Stevanovic?

utterances.speaker: VLASTIMIR DJORDJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were assistant -- assistant ministers, both he and I. We were on a par, to put it that way. We both received orders from the minister regardless of the fact that at that point in time according to the official decision I was the chief of the public security structure, nevertheless, I couldn't issue Obrad Stevanovic with a single order since we were both assistant ministers. He could receive orders solely from the minister, not from me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we bring up 65 ter number 0600 [sic]. And this is the record of what Mr. Stevanovic said in his suspect -- what I want to ask you now -- about -- it's 65 ter number 06000.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, again we're dealing with the interview with a suspect. This time it's Mr. Obrad Stevanovic. I would like to check in advance, or, rather, to prevent the possibility that this is dealt in the same manner as earlier statements of suspects. Mr. Obrad Stevanovic was on the Prosecution's list of witnesses, but the Prosecution eventually gave up on examining him. So I would like to know about the procedure with regard to the use of such statements. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Your question could involve a chapter of a book on evidence, Mr. Djurdjic, and we won't go into that. What was done by Mr. Stamp earlier today is in accordance with the procedures which we accept and in our understanding is not at all contrary to what was said on the -- in the decision in June to which you referred earlier. There are limited uses that can be made and limited uses of such material for our purposes. They mainly go to credit, not substantive evidence.
